body.text: Just under two weeks before a scheduled National Press Club address to unveil his immigration overhaul, home affairs minister Tony Burke gave his department written directions aimed at slowing down visa approvals.

It was Friday 24 July, right in the middle of the Labor Party’s fiftieth national conference in Adelaide. It was also the day before delegates were due to vote on a resolution in Burke’s ministerial patch. Subject to last-minute negotiations, the resolution would open a debate about one of Labor’s most historically sensitive issues: refugees.

Burke’s go-slow documents involved family and skilled-migrant visas, not refugees, but the overarching issue was immigration, and specifically numbers. With One Nation’s siren song draining major parties’ support, immigration had again taken an outsized role in national politics. And that debate is all about numbers.

Exactly eight weeks later, the minister would revoke one of the directions he issued that day, signing a replacement to effectively reverse it. In between, he had been forced to postpone his Press Club speech after cabinet colleagues declined to endorse what he’d planned to announce; he’d copped a public intervention from prime minister Anthony Albanese after a newspaper suggested he was cutting the refugee intake unannounced; and he’d finally unveiled a revised policy while pretending nothing had gone wrong.
Within Labor, views differ about whether blame for this messy sequence lies ultimately with Albanese, Burke or both.

Tony Burke has been under pressure to lower the annual net overseas migration figure, or NOM — arrivals minus departures — and save money. “We are bringing migration down with a sensible, measured approach to provide the skilled workers Australia needs, while addressing exploitation and rorts,” he had declared in mid June, as he revealed new figures showing a fall of 9 per cent, to 301,000, for the previous calendar year. He emphasised how far they’d fallen since their post-Covid peak in 2023.

The government had vowed to lower the NOM to 225,000 within two years, mindful that Australia’s falling fertility rate and a private sector desperate for workers mean cutting migration too much harder risks tanking the economy. Business agrees, but Labor’s opponents wanted more. In the weeks that followed, they would outline their own dramatically lower targets, absent any costings. One Nation would go first, in September, the Coalition two weeks ago.

Against this backdrop, Burke’s proxies at the Adelaide conference were negotiating on the wording of the proposed resolution from the party-faithful group Labor for Refugees. The advocates had lost their fight to secure platform amendments locking in both the size of the refugee intake and a standing pledge to increase it. The signs were worrying given the minister had privately lamented the program’s cost and the government was wary of right-wing campaigning on refugees. In lieu of written commitments, the group planned to take the resolution to the conference floor on Saturday morning.

While those backroom negotiations continued through Friday, Burke was quietly executing other elements of his complicated immigration workover. Burke’s plan would come a bit unstuck. But that July Friday in Adelaide, things were still on course. More or less.

Labor’s platform is the policy guidebook for its parliamentarians, updated at each triennial conference and most consequential when the party is governing and must actually deliver what it promises. It doesn’t compel ministers, but they can’t defy it outright. So the drafting gets close attention.

Labor for Refugees had wanted the 2026 platform to confirm the existing annual refugee intake of 20,000 and restate the party’s intention to progressively reach 27,000, amid fears the minister was backtracking on both. Burke wanted wiggle room. In a year’s time, if nothing changed, the intake would be reduced because it hadn’t formally been extended. But he didn’t want to commit either way.

Formal negotiations over the wording had gone on for months through Labor’s national policy forum. The draft resolution had replaced the 2023 commitment to “increase” refugee numbers with a pledge simply to “maintain a generous humanitarian intake.” The word “increase” had entered through the same process before the 2023 conference, as a pointed message to Albanese’s government. Albanese had gone to the 2022 election promising to raise the intake to 20,000 after Scott Morrison’s Coalition government cut it from 18,750 to 13,750 in 2020. But, more than a year since winning office, he hadn’t done it.

Before the 2023 conference, with the “increase” pledge about to be entrenched, Albanese moved to head off trouble. Exactly one week out, the then immigration minister, Andrew Giles, suddenly announced the promised rise. It was a pre-emptive manoeuvre Albanese would use again before this year’s conference to quell unrest over artificial intelligence. This time, he gave a speech just days before, laying out his proposed AI agenda and promising legislated standards, successfully muting grievances about regulation, jobs and copyright law. Back in 2023, the oil-on-troubled-waters move dealt with refugees.

“The Albanese government reaffirms its commitment to those in need with an increase in our humanitarian program annual intake,” Giles said in his August 2023 media release. “This responsibility extends beyond their arrival, by providing robust support to refugees to ensure they are well equipped to settle into Australia and rebuild their lives with certainty.”

Three years on, Albanese and Burke didn’t want to repeat that explicit promise. Burke was dealing with the smoke-and-mirrors legacy of Giles’s announcement, and the Morrison government’s before that. In its October 2020 budget — delayed from May by pandemic lockdowns — the Coalition had slashed the intake to 13,750 then masked the cut’s severity in 2021–22 with a temporary top-up of 4125 extra places reserved for Afghans fleeing the resurgent Taliban. Giles announced he was raising the intake from 17,875 to 20,000, seemingly an increase of 2125 places. But his baseline figure included the Afghan allocation, which was actually finishing. The true baseline was 13,750, so the real increase was 6250 places. That was going to be expensive.

Four months later, the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook revealed the cost: $641.5 million, minus an estimated $55 million that would flow back to the economy when the refugees got jobs and paid tax. Crucially, the boost was funded for just four years. Without a formal decision before the end of 2026–27 to roll it over, it would expire. By this July’s conference, a month into the financial year, no decision had been made about numbers beyond the year.

Just why not is the subject of speculation. Most budget measures are on a four-year funding cycle and governments sometimes delay formally extending them. This can happen when an election is due before the program’s scheduled rollover, especially if the opposition is minded to cut it. A confirmation commits future funding, which opponents can then bank as a saving or repurpose for an alternative promise; safer to stay noncommittal, removing the funding from the budget papers until it’s renewed and denying that campaign-costings windfall.

The next federal election isn’t due until 2028 but the delay manoeuvre has other useful applications, such as enabling fence-sitting through a party conference, improving the budget’s bottom line and reducing the NOM, at least temporarily. The refugee intake is totemic for Labor; confirming a reduction pre-conference would invite an uprising like the one Albanese led against then leader Bill Shorten on the same issue in 2015. Now prime minister, he couldn’t champion a cut.

But the conservative parties’ resonant anti-immigrant narrative meant declaring the intake was staying at 20,000 could invite a broader backlash with electoral consequences. It might also be hard-fought in cabinet, where everyone was watching the cost of everything. If skilfully handled, the indecision tactic would avoid some of that. It also meant the budget papers would have to show a funding drop-off after this year because no more money had been committed.

That’s what happened in May. The budget documents revealed a $160 million reduction in refugee, humanitarian settlement and migrant services next year and roughly the same for the three following. Asylum-seeker advocates grew more alarmed when departmental officials started mentioning how expensive resettlement is and were persistently refusing to confirm the intake would be maintained.

Labor for Refugees began mobilising, as they had in 2023. Burke, his staff and assistant minister Julian Hill would have to negotiate to excise language from the platform that could read as commitment. The language might imply they were letting the numbers slide back, but it must not be definitive either way. And they weren’t confirming or denying anything.

The draft still contained one problematic statement: that Labor “aspires to progressively increase Australia’s government-funded humanitarian intake to 27,000 places per year.” Aspiration isn’t commitment, but any reference to “progressively” increasing was tricky. Labor for Refugees wanted to sharpen the pledge and Burke needed to blunt it just enough to be ambiguous.

Having cut their losses, the group still wanted the special resolution, and associated debate, on the Saturday morning agenda. The resolution congratulated the government for the 2023 increase and urged it to maintain the intake at 20,000 “whilst continuing to progress towards achieving 27,000 places per year.”

Hill was doing the negotiating, and on Friday night he made a concession. He offered to turn the group’s resolution from sentiment to substance by converting it to a platform amendment, in return for some caveated language. It would become a pledge not exactly to maintain the current intake but just to “seek, in the short term” to maintain it. The phrase “in the short term” was odd but unexplained. And rather than aspiring to “progressively increase” the intake to 27,000, the party would be “continuing to aspire” to achieve it — with nothing that could be construed as measurable benchmarks. Labor for Refugees accepted the changes, clumsy wording and all.

The next morning, its national co-convenor Peter Lynch commended the amendment to the conference. “Labor for Refugees understands the budgetary and other pressures the government is under in relation to this program,” a surprisingly conciliatory Lynch told delegates, conceding he understood there were “limits to how much can be done.” He spoke of the value in “maintaining” the intake without acknowledging that the platform didn’t quite promise that.

He was remarkably sympathetic to the constraints of a minister he seemed to suggest might still reduce the intake. Although he would later tell his group’s members the amendment was “a win,” his speech still pointedly suggested maybe it wasn’t.

“We’ve noted the forward projections in the budget papers,” he said. “In the coming months, the government will decide on the size of the program from July 2027. We understand there are pressures to reduce the intake back to the Coalition levels.”

And he hinted at what sounded like research suggesting voters were sympathetic to refugees. “Despite the noise from some on the political right, there is every indication that most of the population strongly support the refugee humanitarian program,” he said.

The Saturday morning amendment attracted next-to-no media attention. It passed unremarked and the negotiations went unreported, other than by Labor for Refugees back to its membership. In a post-conference bulletin, the group’s representatives called the amendment “good news and a positive outcome.” They also described specifically how Burke had seeded their fears months earlier.

“At one stage,” they wrote, “after meeting with Minister Burke late last year, we were concerned that the Government would drop this clause from the Platform, due to budgetary considerations and because Labor did not want to be targeted by the Right re the number of refugee intake.”

Over four years, the budgeted annual saving of roughly $160 million to which Lynch alluded adds up to about $641 million — what the 2023 rise had cost. Burke downplayed the funding drop-off as the natural end of a funding cycle but was carefully non-committal beyond it. In late August, the Australian Financial Review reported that a cut was coming and the lower refugee numbers had been factored into the NOM calculation. Taken together, it looked like an undisclosed plan, without cabinet approval, to reduce the intake by attrition — which was what the AFR reported it was. If Burke was still planning to ask cabinet to maintain it, then both the savings and the banked NOM deflation were temporary, arguably even artificial.

Burke did have other plans for the humanitarian program. Home Affairs was certainly under budgetary pressure, especially given the portfolio’s security imperatives had only increased since December’s Bondi Beach terrorist attack. As officials had been suggesting, the humanitarian program is costly and has become a magnet for rorters because of the rights it bestows. Claiming asylum is now a favoured way for people on other expiring visas to extend their stay, despite many hailing from stable democracies with no prima facie grounds to fear persecution.

The minister wanted to tighten access to the program, limit capacity to challenge rejection and reduce costs. He wanted to make it harder to lodge frivolous asylum claims by setting a deadline for lodgement, stripping claimants of work rights, and restricting access to review if a claim failed. It was all meant as a disincentive to those just trying it on.

Burke could seek to do this using his regulatory powers. But for every creative mechanism he devised, and every instrument he signed, people found new loopholes. Instead, he planned to persuade the Coalition to back legislation to block bogus applicants and make life harder for those tying up the system to spin out their stay. He reasoned it was in the interests of all parties of government to achieve that, so surely the Liberals and Nationals would agree.

They didn’t, so creative application it was. His plans for the asylum system haven’t yet been finalised. As another Labor figure put it: “Rather than look for the silver bullet, he’s having to find coins down the back of the couch.”
That endeavour encountered another challenge, this time from within the government.

In the weeks leading up to his original Press Club booking, Burke had taken his matrix of proposed changes to cabinet’s expenditure review committee. There was back and forth, and some resistance. Days before the speech, his colleagues withheld final signoff. It’s understood he complained to others that the feedback could have been clearer, sooner.

One person familiar with the events described Burke’s documentation for the committee as “a bit translucent” and “thin.” It’s understood that Treasurer Jim Chalmers and others questioned how thoroughly the plan had been costed, especially measures to restrict work rights. Concerns were raised that asylum applicants would be entitled to government support if they couldn’t work to support themselves. Rather than saving money, that could end up costing the taxpayer upwards of $1.5 billion. But colleagues also challenged his proposed explanation of the whole package. Some felt it didn’t articulate clearly enough why measures that might seem harsh were so necessary, or what they were designed to achieve.

The ABC was first to report that the speech was off, quoting Burke’s spokesperson saying it had been postponed because it had become clear that “some elements of the speech would not be finalised by Thursday.”

Some in the wider Labor caucus were also unhappy when they learned about the visa go-slow strategy, especially for skilled workers. One described the shorter priority list as “strangling the pathways we needed.” Complaints started rolling in. A hospital couldn’t bring in the specialist it urgently required. A big bank couldn’t get a visa for its new executive.

Three weeks after the speech was cancelled, while Burke was still revamping his approach, the report by the AFR’s Phillip Coorey landed, suggesting he was intending to let the refugee intake fall back from 20,000 to 13,750, which would further contravene the promise to rank-and-file party members, which Albanese had helped secure in 2015, to reach 27,000 by 2025. Coorey reported that Burke’s office had confirmed the cut.

By late afternoon, apparently seeking to head off a party backlash that so far hadn’t materialised, Albanese intervened, first in public comments that were not definitive enough and then in an unequivocal statement, sent by text message to the ABC’s Jane Norman. The 20,000 intake would not change.

“The refugee intake needs to be renewed in the coming budget as the 20,000 places was available for four years,” Albanese’s message was reported as saying. “This intake number remains government policy and will be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments and sits beside our strong border security measures.”

Seemingly fitting an emerging pattern of prime ministerial override, Albanese’s intervention was only a one-day story. This was despite it costing Burke’s budget at least $640 million and having implications for everything else he was doing — including those directions to slow visas and help lower the NOM. Those would need to succeed because, next year, there would be 6250 more refugees than the number apparently accounted for. The home affairs minister took it all surprisingly well.

Burke’s spokesperson told Inside Story that he had “always intended to bring forward a submission for the continuation of the humanitarian intake at 20,000.” But discussions had not started “and would normally have occurred in the lead up to the budget in May 2027. When the intake became a topic of public discussion the PM made the decision to avoid months of speculation and bring forward the announcement,” the spokesperson said, with no comment on this pre-empting cabinet.
As to the NOM calculations having reflected a lower refugee number, modelling the expected NOM for the budget’s four-year forward estimates was a matter for Treasury.

When he eventually addressed the Press Club last month, Burke conceded that the measures he was outlining were “not as comprehensive” as he wanted. He explained how “the levers” he had weren’t enough to tackle exploitation comprehensively. “You can’t do that without legislation.”

But his powers weren’t useless. In July, he’d signed those new ministerial directions to put the squeeze on other parts of the migration program and get the politically important NOM numbers down. The directions dramatically contracted the list of priority occupations, putting defence and law enforcement first, then health, teaching and construction. They also amounted to a go-slow on approvals because onshore applicants had to jump ahead of anyone applying from overseas. People already here don’t add to the NOM number. Liberal leader Angus Taylor’s alternative focus on forcing students to leave before applying for visa extensions would have a similar effect. Departures help bring the NOM down too.

Burke had also signed direction 120, which covers “exceptional and outstanding achievement” visas. Replacing a 2024 version, this slightly rearranged the processing order for “exceptional” applications to give greater priority to those working in “critical technologies,” renewable energy and health industries, followed by an expanded list of six other sectors: agrifood and agritech; defence capabilities and space; education; financial services and fintech; infrastructure and transport; and resources.

The new directions were among a web of measures designed not only to further restrict who comes to Australia but also to increase control over who stays and for how long. All of it had been in train since February, he insisted, including the restrictions on foreign students bringing their families and the new priority list for skills. He was introducing ballots for working backpackers wanting to stay longer than a year and a no-further-stay provision for those missing out, with the same provision for other tourists whose visas had expired. The measures to stop visa-hopping were partly about those bogus asylum claims, though he didn’t dwell on that.

But moves aimed at stopping people exploiting Australia’s generosity must be finely tuned to avoid locking out those with genuine and lawful protection claims, robbing the nation of skills it needs or arbitrarily blocking sponsorship of relatives whose arrival could boost whole families’ contributions to the economy and community. Changes to the wider migrant-intake composition can significantly affect the economy and are also politically fraught, making the system notoriously difficult to tweak.

Burke wanted to stop people gaming the rules by using visa rollover provisions to extend their stay with the help of migration agents and lawyers he regards as unscrupulously profiting from such loopholes. That practice has increased, including since the Coalition-negotiated British free trade agreement, which took effect in 2023, has allowed British backpackers to stay up to three years in Australia on a working holiday without meeting the regional job requirements others face. When their work or holiday visas expire, a growing number of these and other foreign citizens are applying for humanitarian protection, buying sometimes years more onshore while their applications wind through bureaucratic and legal processes.

The day after his speech, Burke signed three new ministerial directions. He replaced 119, the skilled-visa go-slow he’d only introduced in July, with directions 121 and 122, separating the rules for temporary and permanent skilled migrant visas. Those upended the narrow priority list that had favoured onshore applicants in defence and law-enforcement. Construction now came first, then healthcare, teaching, agriculture, aquaculture, fishing and resources, whether applicants were here already or overseas, followed by defence and law enforcement. While the next priority level of occupations still favoured onshore applicants, that preference was gone for the most-sought-after skills.

The temporary category now also has exceptions, letting applicants with “compelling circumstances” jump the queue. They include those involved with community safety, essential religious, cultural or community services, or Australia’s international relations. Same for permanent skilled visa applications, minus the international relations. The new directions better address skills shortages and ease caucus concerns but are less helpful in lowering the NOM.

And Burke’s backpacker ballot has drawn a backlash from industries reliant on seasonal workers. Designed to fix one problem, they say it’s created another and will leave them dangerously short. This week the Australian Hotels Association launched a video campaign highlighting the products and services that would be unavailable if the backpacker workforce disappears. While other business associations have targeted the more drastic proposed migration cuts of One Nation and the Coalition, the AHA is targeting Labor as the only party restricting backpackers.

Burke’s third new direction, number 123, covers changes to the rules for refusing or cancelling visas and specifically to the character test. It includes the tougher hate speech provisions that he flagged in his address and elevates concerns about crimes against women and children. It also describes bad-character risks to “the social fabric.” To deny or revoke a visa, a decision-maker previously had to reasonably suspect a person “will” do something untoward, or certain conduct “will” be harmful. Now it’s just if they “might” or “could.”

New character provisions emphasise the Australian community’s expectations with ties to Australia no longer a primary consideration. Overall, the changes in Direction 123 make it easier to reject people on character grounds and to deport them, which could help ensure the NOM still falls, even with the current refugee intake restored.

Still, a small headache for Burke was buried in the new documents. Ministerial direction 123, which doesn’t take effect until 31 October, contains a potentially unhelpful typographical error — a “not” in one clause where there shouldn’t be one.
Yet another problem for the minister to fix. •
